name: Chisel
text: Legal publishes a *time-stamped, auto-approved queue* for repurposed assets, with Product Ops responsible for logging every auto-cleared item. Legal retains the right to audit the queue weekly and retroactively block anything that violates the red-line playbook. This shifts the bottleneck from real-time approval to targeted review, cutting repurposing delays while keeping Legal’s oversight intact. The trade-off: some risky assets may slip through before Legal catches them, but the weekly audit limits exposure and forces Product Ops to justify their decisions.

name: Sift
text: The real risk isn’t edge cases slipping—it’s Product Ops gaming the system by over-escalating trivial issues to avoid accountability. Instead, Legal should publish the playbook but require Product Ops to batch and timestamp edge cases weekly, with Legal reviewing only the batch, not individual requests. This forces discipline without creating a new bottleneck.

name: Scope
text: Legal publishes a single, public "Repurpose Rules Matrix"—a one-page table listing every repurposing rule with a clear yes/no/ask-Legal column. Product Ops runs the queue: if the rule says yes, auto-clear; if no, auto-block; if ask-Legal, escalate with a timestamped log. This cuts Legal’s workload to only the 10% of cases where the matrix forces their hand, while keeping repurposing fast and transparent. Trade-off: the matrix must stay ruthlessly simple—no edge-case exceptions, or Product Ops will exploit gaps to shift blame.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk isn’t Product Ops gaming the system—it’s Legal gaming the system by hiding behind the playbook to avoid making hard calls. Instead, Legal should publish the playbook but *require* Product Ops to flag only the top 5% most ambiguous cases for Legal review—no more, no less. That settles it: clear threshold, measurable load, and Legal can’t duck accountability.

name: Reel
text: Legal publishes a single, immutable "repurposing rules matrix" that auto-approves or auto-blocks every asset based on pre-set criteria—no playbooks, no escalations. Product Ops runs the queue; Legal only reviews exceptions flagged by the matrix. This cuts repurposing time to near-zero while forcing Legal to hard-code their risk tolerance upfront. The trade-off: we lock in today’s rules and accept that tomorrow’s edge cases will require a full matrix update, not ad-hoc fixes.

name: Scriv
text: Legal owning the final call on *all* repurposed assets turns Product Ops into a rubber-stamp bureaucracy—slowing repurposing to a crawl and making them less accountable, not more. The real risk isn’t edge cases slipping; it’s Product Ops weaponizing escalation to shift blame upward, while Legal drowns in trivial reviews. Settle it by making Product Ops *automatically* repurpose when the playbook’s rules are clear, but force them to *publicly* log every deviation—so Legal only reviews the exceptions, not the defaults.

name: Chisel
text: Legal publishes a *time-stamped, auto-approved queue* for repurposed assets, with Legal reserving the right to retroactively pull any item within 72 hours if it violates the playbook. This keeps repurposing fast by trusting Product Ops to act, while giving Legal a safety net to correct mistakes without slowing the pipeline. The trade-off is accepting a small risk of bad assets going live temporarily, but the alternative—Legal reviewing every item upfront—creates a bottleneck that kills speed.

name: Sift
text: The real risk isn’t Product Ops gaming the system—it’s Legal becoming the bottleneck by owning *every* final call. Instead, Legal should publish a playbook with *clear, binary thresholds* for escalation (e.g., "if X, escalate; if Y, auto-clear"), and Product Ops should enforce it with a *public audit trail*. That settles it: no ambiguity, no over-escalation, and Legal only reviews actual gray areas.
